mainTopic: Mistaken sales by an agent, a widow, or a court; the power of בית דין; and who guarantees such sales
overview: The גמרא first asks how to treat an agent (שליח) who sold property at a slightly wrong price. רבא reports in the name of רב נחמן that the agent is like the judges (דיינין), since neither acts for himself. רב שמואל בר ביסנא reports that the agent is like the widow (אלמנה), since both are single individuals, and the הלכה follows this view. A משנה about an agent who separates תרומה seems to give agents leeway. The גמרא explains that תרומה has an accepted range of amounts, while a wrong price is simply a mistake. Next, רב נחמן rules like the חכמים, who hold that a court sale with an error is cancelled. The גמרא reconciles this with his ruling about orphans dividing property: a court that erred can be overturned, but a correct division cannot. Two versions of a story about רבי and פרטא follow, and they differ only on the facts. Finally רב יוסף rules that the orphans carry the guarantee when a widow or a בית דין sells estate land. The explanation of why the בית דין case needed to be said continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Two reports of רב נחמן's ruling on an agent
steps.stepSummary: רבא quotes רב נחמן as saying an agent is like the judges. רב שמואל בר ביסנא quotes him as saying an agent is like the widow.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רב נחמן: an agent is treated like judges. רב שמואל בר ביסנא said in the name of רב נחמן: an agent is treated like a widow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings two different versions of what רב נחמן said about an agent who made a mistake when selling property. The next steps will explain each version.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא gave two models for a sale with a pricing mistake. Judges (דיינין) who sell property get some leeway for a small error, while a widow (אלמנה) selling for her כתובה does not. The question is which model fits an agent (שליח).

keyTerms.meaning: An agent, someone sent to act for another person
Judges of the court (בית דין) who sell property by assessment
A widow, here one who sells her late husband's property to collect her כתובה

phrases.english: Rava said in the name of Rav Naḥman:
An agent is like the judges.

phrases.aramaic: רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר בִּיסְנָא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna said in the name of Rav Naḥman:
He is like a widow.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: שָׁלִיחַ כְּדַיָּינִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new discussion about the agent, building on the earlier cases of judges and a widow.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are two reports of רב נחמן: the agent is compared either to judges or to a widow.

steps.title: Why רבא compares the agent to judges
steps.stepSummary: Judges do not sell for their own benefit, and neither does an agent. The widow is different because she sells for herself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as judges do not act for themselves, an agent also does not act for himself. This leaves out the widow, who acts for herself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats רבא's version and explains its reasoning: the agent, like the judges, is acting for someone else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point they share is that neither has a personal interest in the sale. So the agent gets the same leeway as the judges. The widow is excluded because she sells to collect her own money.

keyTerms.meaning: For themselves, for their own benefit
To leave out, to exclude

phrases.english: Rava said in the name of Rav Naḥman:
An agent is like the judges.
Just as the judges are not acting for themselves —
so too the agent is not acting for himself,
which leaves out the widow, who acts for herself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the first report in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The agent is like the judges because neither acts for his own benefit.

steps.title: Why רב שמואל בר ביסנא compares the agent to a widow
steps.stepSummary: A widow is a single person, and so is an agent. A court is different because it is made up of several people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as a widow is one person, an agent is one person. This leaves out the court, which is made up of many people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the second version and explains its reasoning: the agent, like the widow, is a single individual.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the key feature is a different one: the number of people involved. A court of several judges gets leeway, but a single person does not. So the agent, being one person, is treated strictly like the widow.

keyTerms.meaning: A single individual (feminine form)
Many people, a group

phrases.aramaic: רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר בִּיסְנָא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna said in the name of Rav Naḥman:
He is like a widow; just as a widow is one person —
so too an agent is one person,
which leaves out the court — since they are many.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning of the second report, which competes with the reasoning in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The agent is like the widow because both are single individuals.

steps.title: The הלכה: an agent is like a widow
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules that the agent is treated like the widow.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: an agent is like a widow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא decides between the two versions and follows רב שמואל בר ביסנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the agent is like the widow, he does not get the judges' leeway for a pricing mistake. This ruling is what the next step will challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: And the practical law is

steps.whatToRemember: Two ways to compare the agent: like judges (not for himself) or like a widow (one person). The הלכה: the agent is like a widow.

phrases.english: And the halakha is: an agent is like a widow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides between the two views in steps 2 and 3.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The agent is treated like the widow, so his pricing mistakes are not given leeway.

steps.title: Challenge from an agent who separates תרומה
steps.stepSummary: A משנה says that an agent who separates תרומה and is off by ten in the ratio still has valid תרומה. Why is this agent's mistake tolerated, when an agent who sells property gets no leeway?
steps.simpleTranslation: How is this different from the משנה: If someone tells his agent 'Go and separate תרומה,' the agent separates according to the owner's wishes. If he does not know the owner's wishes, he separates an average amount, one-fiftieth. If he took off ten or added ten, his תרומה is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ruling that an agent is like a widow, using a משנה about an agent separating תרומה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the תרומה case the agent did not do exactly what the owner wanted, yet his act still counts. That seems to give the agent leeway. This clashes with treating an agent strictly, like a widow.

keyTerms.meaning: And how is it different?
The portion of produce given to a כהן
The owner
An average, middle amount

phrases.english: And how is it different from what we learned in a mishna:
One who says to his agent, "Go out and separate terumah" —
he separates according to the owner's wishes,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם אֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ דַּעְתּוֹ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת —
phrases.english: and if he does not know the owner's wishes —
he separates an average amount, one out of fifty.
If he took off ten or added ten,
phrases.notes: He means one out of forty or one out of sixty instead of one out of fifty.

phrases.english: his terumah is valid terumah.

steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that an agent is like a widow and gets no leeway for a mistake.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה lets an agent's תרומה stand even when he went off from the owner's wishes, which suggests agents do get leeway.

steps.title: Why the תרומה agent gets leeway but the selling agent does not
steps.stepSummary: With תרומה there is a normal range of amounts people give, so the agent can say he guessed the owner's style. With a sale, a bad price is just a mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, some people separate תרומה stingily and some generously, so the agent can tell the owner: 'That is how I judged you.' But here, it is simply a mistake, so the owner can tell the agent: 'You should not have made a mistake.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 5 by showing that the two cases are not alike.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In תרומה there is no single correct amount, because both a stingy and a generous amount are acceptable. So the agent's 'mistake' can be read as a choice about what the owner would want. In a sale there is one fair price, so getting it wrong is a real error and the owner can cancel.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'a bad eye': giving stingily, the smallest normal amount of תרומה
Literally 'a good eye': giving generously, the larger normal amount of תרומה
I estimated you, meaning I judged what kind of giver you are
A mistake, an error

steps.whatToRemember: An agent's choice inside an accepted range counts as a valid estimate. A plain error outside the fair value is not forgiven.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם כֵּיוָן דְּאִיכָּא דְּתוֹרֵם בְּעַיִן רָעָה
phrases.english: There, since there are those who separate תרומה with a 'bad eye'
phrases.notes: 'There' is the תרומה case from the משנה quoted in step 5. A 'bad eye' means a stingy giver.

phrases.english: and there are those who separate with a 'good eye,'
he can say to him: That is how I judged you.
But here, it is a mistake,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לֵיהּ: לָא אִיבְּעִי לָךְ לְמִיטְעֵי.
phrases.english: so he can say to him: You should not have made a mistake.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם כֵּיוָן דְּאִיכָּא דְּתוֹרֵם בְּעַיִן רָעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 5
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between the cases (חילוק): a range of acceptable choices versus a real error
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both agents made a miscalculation, so both should be treated the same
steps.terutzMaskana: The תרומה agent acted within an accepted range and can claim he estimated the owner; the selling agent simply erred

steps.title: רב נחמן rules like the חכמים
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר חנינא reports that רב נחמן rules like the חכמים in the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר חנינא said in the name of רב נחמן: The הלכה follows the חכמים.
steps.whatsHappening: A new section starts: the גמרא brings a ruling of רב נחמן on the dispute in the משנה. This sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the חכמים hold that when judges sell and make a significant error, the sale is cancelled. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds the sale stands, because otherwise 'what advantage is there to the court's power?' רב נחמן sides with the חכמים.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical law follows the view of the Sages

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בַּר חֲנִינָא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן,
phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Chanina said that Rav Nachman said:
The halacha follows the words of the Sages.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בַּר חֲנִינָא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new topic: the practical ruling on the משנה's dispute
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows the חכמים: a court's sale with a significant error is cancelled

steps.title: רב נחמן seems to agree with the idea of the court's special power
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן: in the case of orphans dividing property, he himself says they cannot protest once grown, using the very argument of 'what advantage is there to the court's power.'
steps.simpleTranslation: But doesn't רב נחמן hold the idea 'what advantage is there to the court's power'? Didn't רב נחמן say in the name of שמואל: When orphans come to divide their father's property, the court appoints a guardian for them, and the court chooses a fair portion for each. Once they grow up, they can protest. And רב נחמן himself said: Once they grow up, they cannot protest, because if they could, what advantage would there be to the court's power?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב נחמן's ruling from step 7 by showing he uses רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's reasoning in another case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ruling like the חכמים means a court's action can be undone. But in the orphans case, רב נחמן says the court's division cannot be undone, exactly because a court must have special power. That looks like a contradiction in רב נחמן's own views.

keyTerms.meaning: What advantage is there to the court's power? The argument that a court's actions should be stronger than a private person's
A guardian appointed to manage property for orphans
They grew up, became adults
To protest, to object and try to undo something

steps.confusionAlert: There are two different statements here. שמואל (quoted by רב נחמן) says the grown orphans CAN protest. רב נחמן's own view is that they CANNOT. The challenge is built on רב נחמן's own view.

phrases.english: But doesn't Rav Nachman hold
'What advantage is there to the court's power?'
But didn't Rav Nachman say that Shmuel said:
Orphans who came to divide their father's property —
the court appoints a guardian for them,
and they choose for them a fair portion.
Once they grew up, they can protest.
And Rav Nachman himself said:
Once they grew up, they cannot protest,

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֵּן מָה כֹּחַ בֵּית דִּין יָפֶה.
phrases.english: for if so, what advantage is there to the court's power?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵית לֵיהּ לְרַב נַחְמָן מָה כֹּחַ בֵּית דִּין יָפֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of step 7 from רב נחמן's own statement elsewhere
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling like the חכמים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Contradiction: in the orphans case רב נחמן uses רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's argument that a court's action cannot be undone

steps.title: A court that erred versus a court that did not
steps.stepSummary: The two rulings of רב נחמן deal with different cases: in the משנה the judges erred, and in the orphans case they did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult: this case is where they made a mistake, and that case is where they did not make a mistake.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by saying each ruling of רב נחמן is about a different situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When judges actually erred, as in the משנה, רב נחמן agrees the sale is cancelled, like the חכמים. When the court did not err, as in dividing the orphans' property fairly, the court's power holds and the orphans cannot protest.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; the standard opening of an answer that resolves a contradiction
This one ... that one; used to split two sources into two different cases

phrases.english: It is not difficult: this is where they erred,
that is where they did not err.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דִּטְעוֹ, הָא דְּלָא טְעוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the two sources into different cases (erred vs. did not err)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב נחמן contradicts himself about whether a court's action can be undone
steps.terutzMaskana: A court's error can be undone; a court's correct action cannot be challenged

steps.title: If the court did not err, what is there to protest?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the court divided correctly, what complaint would the orphans even have, according to שמואל who says they can protest?
steps.simpleTranslation: If they did not make a mistake, about what could the orphans protest?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the answer from step 9, asking what a protest could be about if the division was correct. This sets up the final answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 9 says the orphans case has no error. But שמואל said grown orphans can protest, so there must be something to object to. The גמרא wants to know what that could be.

keyTerms.meaning: About what? In what way?

phrases.english: If they did not err,
about what can they protest?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי דְּלָא טְעוֹ, בְּמַאי יְכוֹלִין לְמַחוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case-definition given in step 9
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the orphans case is one where the court did not err
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If nothing went wrong, שמואל's statement that grown orphans can protest seems to have no content

steps.title: They can protest about the locations
steps.stepSummary: Even with fair values, an orphan can object to where his share was placed.
steps.simpleTranslation: About the directions, meaning the locations of the fields each one received.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the protest is not about value but about location.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each share may be worth the right amount, yet one orphan may prefer land on a different side or in a different place. שמואל allows that kind of protest, while רב נחמן holds that a correct court division stands even against that.

keyTerms.meaning: Directions, sides; here, the locations of the plots of land

steps.whatToRemember: רב נחמן follows the חכמים when a court truly errs, but holds that a court's correct action cannot be challenged. 'Did not err' means fair value, even if someone prefers a different location.

phrases.english: About the directions.
phrases.notes: He means the location of each plot. An orphan might say, 'I wanted the field on the other side.'

steps.terutzResolutionType: Clarifying the content of the protest
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the division was fair, there is nothing to protest
steps.terutzMaskana: The protest can be about which location each orphan received, even when the values were correct

steps.title: רב דימי's report: רבי ruled, then reversed
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports that רבי once ruled like the חכמים. פרטא objected, 'If so, what advantage does the court have?', and רבי reversed his ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he said: There was a case, and רבי ruled like the חכמים. פרטא, the son of רבי אלעזר בן פרטא and grandson of רבי פרטא הגדול, said to him: If so, what advantage does the court's power have? And רבי reversed his ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a real-life story, reported by רב דימי, about how רבי actually ruled on this question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי first followed the חכמים of the משנה. פרטא pushed back with the very argument the משנה uses for the other side: a court must have more power than an ordinary person. Convinced, רבי took back a ruling he had already made.

keyTerms.meaning: When [he] came, usually from ארץ ישראל to בבל, bringing a teaching
A real case or incident
What advantage does the court's power have (over an ordinary person)?
Reversed, took back (a ruling)

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came, he said:
There was an incident, and Rabbi acted according to the words of the Rabbis,
phrases.notes: 'רבי' here means רבי יהודה הנשיא, and the 'Rabbis' are the חכמים in our משנה.

phrases.english: Perata said before him,

phrases.aramaic: בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן פַּרְטָא
phrases.english: the son of Rabbi Elazar ben Perata,

phrases.aramaic: בֶּן בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי פַּרְטָא הַגָּדוֹל:
phrases.english: the grandson of Rabbi Perata the Great:

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֵּן מָה כֹּחַ בֵּית דִּין יָפֶה,
phrases.english: If so, what advantage is there to the power of the court?
And Rabbi reversed the ruling in the incident.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי, אָמַר: מַעֲשֶׂה וְעָשָׂה רַבִּי כְּדִבְרֵי חֲכָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a real case in which רבי dealt with the dispute of the משנה that רב נחמן ruled on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ruled like the חכמים, then reversed that ruling after פרטא's objection.

steps.title: רב ספרא's version: רבי never ruled at all
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא tells the story differently: רבי only wanted to rule like the חכמים, and after פרטא's objection he never carried it out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב דימי teaches it this way. רב ספרא teaches it this way: There was a case, and רבי wanted to rule like the חכמים. פרטא said to him: If so, what advantage does the court's power have? So רבי did not act on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the same story, from רב ספרא, which changes one key detail.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב דימי's version רבי actually ruled and then reversed. In רב ספרא's version רבי only intended to rule, so there was never a ruling to take back. This difference sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: Teaches (reports) it this way
Wanted to act (but had not yet acted)

steps.confusionAlert: Both versions agree on the ending, that רבי did not finally rule like the חכמים. The only difference is whether he had already given a ruling before changing course.

phrases.english: Rav Dimi teaches it this way;
Rav Safra teaches it this way:
There was an incident, and Rabbi wished
to act according to the words of the Rabbis.
Perata said before him,

phrases.aramaic: בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן פַּרְטָא
phrases.english: the son of Rabbi Elazar ben Perata,

phrases.aramaic: בֶּן בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי פַּרְטָא הַגָּדוֹל:
phrases.english: the grandson of Rabbi Perata the Great:

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֵּן מָה כֹּחַ בֵּית דִּין יָפֶה?
phrases.english: If so, what advantage is there to the power of the court?
Rabbi did not carry out the ruling.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב דִּימִי מַתְנֵי הָכִי, רַב סָפְרָא מַתְנֵי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different version of the same story told in step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי only intended to rule like the חכמים and never did, because of פרטא's objection.

steps.title: Suggestion: the versions differ over reversing an error in a דבר משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the two versions reflect a real legal dispute: can a judge who erred in a 'דבר משנה' reverse his ruling?
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this is what they disagree about? One holds that if a judge made a mistake in a matter of משנה, the ruling is reversed. The other holds that it is not reversed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether the two versions of the story are really two opinions about a point of law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב דימי's version, where רבי reversed after ruling, fits the view that a mistake in a 'דבר משנה' can be reversed. רב ספרא's version, where רבי stopped before ruling, might mean that once he ruled he could not have reversed. That would explain why רב ספרא tells it that way.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (introduces a suggestion the גמרא may later reject)
They disagree
Erred in a matter of משנה, a mistake against an established, known law
Is reversed (the ruling is undone)

phrases.english: Shall we say that they disagree about this:

phrases.aramaic: מָר סָבַר: טָעָה בִּדְבַר מִשְׁנָה — חוֹזֵר,
phrases.english: One Sage holds: if he erred in a matter of Mishnah, the ruling is reversed,
phrases.notes: This is רב דימי, which is why in his version רבי could take back a ruling he had already given.

phrases.english: and the other Sage holds: it is not reversed.
phrases.notes: This is רב ספרא, so in his version רבי had to stop before ruling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a legal reason behind the factual difference between steps 12 and 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do רב דימי and רב ספרא disagree about whether a judge's error in a דבר משנה is reversed?

steps.title: Rejection: everyone agrees, they only differ on the facts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. Everyone agrees an error in a 'דבר משנה' is reversed, and רב דימי and רב ספרא only disagree about what happened in the story.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees that if a judge erred in a matter of משנה, the ruling is reversed. One just holds the story happened this way, and the other holds it happened that way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own suggestion and says there is no legal dispute here at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both agree on the law: a mistake in a 'דבר משנה' can be undone. Their difference is only historical, about whether רבי had already ruled or only planned to. So the two versions teach us nothing about a dispute in law.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees
This is how the incident happened

steps.whatToRemember: Two versions of a story do not always mean two legal opinions. Here everyone holds that a judge's error in a 'דבר משנה' is reversed, and רב דימי and רב ספרא only differ on the facts of what רבי did.

phrases.english: No, everyone agrees:
if he erred in a matter of Mishnah, the ruling is reversed.
And one Sage holds the incident happened this way,
and the other Sage holds the incident happened that way.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא טָעָה בִּדְבַר מִשְׁנָה חוֹזֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 14's suggestion of a legal dispute.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that רב דימי and רב ספרא disagree about the law of a judge's error in a דבר משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The suggestion assumed the different versions came from different legal views, but they are only different memories of the facts.

steps.title: The orphans carry the guarantee for sales by a widow or a court
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף rules that if a widow sells estate property, or a בית דין sells it, the orphans are responsible for the buyer's guarantee.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: When a widow sells property, the guarantee is on the orphans. And when a בית דין sells property, the guarantee is also on the orphans.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling from רב יוסף about who must pay back a buyer if land sold from the estate is later taken away from him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A widow sells land from her late husband's estate to collect her כתובה or her support. If an earlier creditor later takes that land from the buyer, רב יוסף says the buyer is repaid from the orphans' property, because it was really the estate that was sold. The same rule applies when a בית דין does the selling.

keyTerms.meaning: Guarantee: the duty to repay a buyer if the land he bought is taken away from him
A widow (Aramaic for אַלְמָנָה)
Orphans, the heirs of the late husband
Who sold

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule for buyers: when they buy from a widow or a בית דין, their protection comes from the orphans' estate.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
A widow who sold
the guarantee is upon the orphans.
phrases.notes: If an earlier creditor takes the land from the buyer, the buyer gets repaid from the orphans' property.

phrases.english: And a court that sold
the guarantee is upon the orphans.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic after the discussion of רבי's reversed ruling ends in step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a widow or a בית דין sells estate property, the guarantee to the buyer rests on the orphans.

steps.title: Isn't this obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that רב יוסף's ruling seems too obvious to need saying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יוסף: why would he need to tell us something so clear?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The widow is not selling her own land. She is selling the husband's land, which now belongs to the orphans, to pay his debt to her. So of course the guarantee falls on the orphans.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious: the גמרא asks why a ruling needed to be said at all

steps.confusionAlert: "פשיטא" does not mean the ruling is wrong. The גמרא agrees with it and only asks why it needed to be said.

phrases.english: Isn't it obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for רב יוסף's ruling in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for רב יוסף's statement
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since the widow and the בית דין are selling the estate's land, it is self-evident that the estate, now owned by the orphans, carries the guarantee.

steps.title: The widow case is obvious, but the court case is needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the widow case really is obvious. רב יוסף needed to teach the case of the בית דין, and the גמרא begins to explain what we might have wrongly thought.
steps.simpleTranslation: The widow case was not needed. Where it was needed was the case of the בית דין, because you might have said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits that the widow case is obvious and says the real point is the בית דין case. Then it starts a "you might have thought" line, setting up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer narrows the חידוש of רב יוסף's ruling to the sale by a בית דין. The words מהו דתימא show that there was a reasonable mistaken view about a בית דין sale, which the גמרא is about to spell out.

keyTerms.meaning: It was not needed: this part teaches nothing new
Where it was needed: this points to the real חידוש
Lest you say: introduces a mistaken assumption that the ruling comes to reject

phrases.english: The widow was not necessary for him.
Where it was necessary for him was the court
lest you say:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the חידוש to one part of the ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought a sale by a בית דין works differently from a widow's sale when it comes to the guarantee. The reason is given in the next line.
steps.terutzMaskana: The guarantee rests on the orphans even when a בית דין sold the property.
